title: Who gives amrit
hookLine: five amritdhari Sikhs, with a sixth attending the Granth

lines: A CLOSED DOOR, A QUIET ROOM.
cards: A door is closed. Not locked, just closed, so the room stays quiet. Inside, the Guru Granth Sahib rests open, and one Sikh sits beside it.
Five more stand together, wearing the five Ks, washed and ready. Six people and the book. That's the whole staff.

Nobody arrives from a head office; nobody signs a certificate for an institution. Yesterday's big idea, the Guru Panth, shrinks here to the size of one room, on the day someone new is about to join. So who gives amrit?

teach.h: ANY QUIET PLACE, THE GRANTH PRESENT.
teach.b: The Sikh Rehat Maryada answers plainly. In paraphrase: the initiation may be held in any quiet, suitable place. Besides the Guru Granth Sahib, six Sikhs need to be present.
One attends the Granth. Five give the amrit. Start with the one.
Their task is to sit in attendance on the Guru Granth Sahib, which Sikhs honor as the Guru present in the room.
The ceremony doesn't happen while the book waits on a shelf; it happens in the Guru's presence, with someone caring for that presence the whole time. Then the five.

teach.h: FIVE WHO HAVE TAKEN AMRIT THEMSELVES.
teach.b: The code asks that they be Sikhs who have taken amrit themselves, who keep the five Ks, and who live by the code. You can only pass on what you have received.

Nobody gives amrit on the strength of a title, a degree or a family name; the five give it because they already stand inside the promise they're about to offer. Now the number. The code asks for five, not one.
Together they stand in for the panj pyare, the five beloved ones of Anandpur, whom this path met long ago.
So the authority in the room doesn't belong to any one of them; it sits between them.
And the five aren't a fixed set of people. Any five who meet the code's terms can be chosen for the day. Another month, another town, five different Sikhs, and the amrit is the same amrit.
So the answer isn't a single who. It's a five.

how: Under the Sikh Rehat Maryada, amrit is given in a quiet place in the presence of the Guru Granth Sahib by five amritdhari Sikhs who keep the code, while a sixth Sikh attends the Granth.

o: the head granthi of the local gurdwara, alone
five initiated Sikhs, while a sixth attends the Granth
any elder from the family of the one joining

games.q: the room where amrit is given: tap the pairs.
p: the five beloved ones of Anandpur

s: one priest gives amrit on his own
the code asks for five Sikhs giving it together, with a sixth attending the Granth.
the five must have taken amrit themselves
they keep the five Ks and live by the code: you pass on what you've received.
the same five people must always give it
any five who meet the code's terms can be chosen for the day.

games.q: a gurdwara is planning an amrit ceremony. who does the Sikh code ask to give the amrit?
o: five amritdhari Sikhs who keep the code, together.
anyone in the sangat who volunteers.
games.why: five Sikhs who have taken amrit and keep the code give it together, with a sixth attending the Granth. the authority sits between them.

practice: Picture the room: the Granth open, one person seated beside it, and five standing together with no one in front of the others, and let your attention rest on each of the five in turn; a shape is enough, no faces needed.
Then bring to mind something good you've only ever received from a group, a team, a family table, a crew that covered for you once, and stay with it.

wordCard.voice: Who gives amrit. Five Sikhs who have taken amrit themselves give it together, while a sixth attends the Guru Granth Sahib. Today's word.

orig.note: Punjabi: the five beloved ones. the five who give amrit stand in for them.

carryVoice: Your line: the five give. You can only pass on what you've received. See you tomorrow.
